title: What is known about 1RB0RB_1LB0LC_1RD1LC_1RE0RA_0RF1RA_---1LB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RB_1LB0LC_1RD1LC_1RE0RA_0RF1RA_---1LB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced in Lean to a Collatz-like map. Sampled with the head at the left end, the tape is a run of ones with one hole: p ones, the hole, r ones. Lean proves, for all p, r ≥ 1, that one sample leads to the next by an explicit map f (division of p by 3 when p ≡ 2 mod 3, a jump of the hole to the right end otherwise) in an explicit number of steps, or halts (p = 2 with r divisible by 3), and that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (3, 1) under f reaches that halting case. Following the proved map, the kernel shows no halt in the first 103747 steps. Whether the orbit ever hits the halting case is a Collatz-like question; heuristically the chance is about 10-4.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The halting family
claims.text: With the head in C on the leftmost cell of 1 1 0 1^(3m+3) and blank tape around, the machine reaches F on a 0 with blank tape to its right in 5m + 21 steps and halts there, for every m.

claims.title: The hole map, for all p and r
claims.text: Write S(p, r) for the head in state C on the leftmost cell of 1^p 0 1^r, blank tape around. For all p, r ≥ 1: S(1, r) → S(r+4, 1); S(2, 3m+1) → S(3m+6, 1); S(2, 3m+2) → S(3m+5, 2); S(2, 3m+3) halts; S(3k+3, r) → S(4k+r+6, 1); S(3k+4, r) → S(4k+r+8, 1); S(3k+5, r) → S(k+1, 2k+r+5), each in an exact number of steps cost p r (quadratic in k: a block drifts right over the ones, then is consumed 111 by 111). Built from 15 symbolic rules found and proved by bbtools.symtm, chained by induction over the drift, the consumption and the division rounds.

claims.title: The reduction
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches S(3, 1) in 11 steps, and it halts if and only if the orbit of (3, 1) under the map reaches the halting case p = 2, 3 | r.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>3747</sup> steps
claims.text: The kernel follows the proved map for 30,000 samples from S(3, 1) (the numbers reach 1,874 digits) and adds up the proved step counts: more than 10<sup>3747</sup> steps, none of them a halt.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 18,652 cells have been visited and 18,650 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.068). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.524).

claims.title: The hole map, checked
claims.text: From each sample (C on the leftmost cell, reading 1; N cells, a single 0 at position p): p ≡ 0, p ≥ 3: N' = N + p/3 + 3, p' = N' − 2; p ≡ 1: N' = N + (p−1)/3 + 4, p' = N' − 2; p ≡ 2, p ≥ 5: N' = N + 1, p' = (p−2)/3; p = 2: halt if 3 | N, else N' = N + 4, p' = N' − 2 (N ≡ 1) or N' = N + 3, p' = N' − 3 (N ≡ 2). The machine follows this from every sample with N < 120 and 1 ≤ p ≤ N−2 (exhaustive), along the run for the first 3·10<sup>7</sup> steps (27 samples), and at all 45 samples of the run to 1.9·10<sup>10</sup> steps. (Now proved for all N: see above; this check also confirms the step counts.)

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c: 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt (59,927 ones). The map from the run's first sample (N, p) = (5, 3), iterated 30,000 times (N then has 1,874 digits), never visits p = 2.

claims.title: No closed tape language from windows up to 7
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with K = 2 to 7 closes but allows a halt (7 to 386 abstract halting configurations); n-gram CPS (widths 3 to 7, -H, -U) fails, as it must: the halting family above is real.

claims.title: Why it probably never halts
claims.text: A division chain p → (p−2)/3 → … ends at 2 only if it starts at p = 3<sup>k</sup> − 1, and chains start at N − 2 or N − 3 with N growing by a factor about 4/3 per step. So the run would have to land exactly on one of the sparse numbers 3<sup>k</sup> + 1 (and then pass a test mod 3). Treating N as random at its scale, the expected number of such hits beyond N ≈ 10<sup>5</sup> is about Σ<sub>k≥11</sub> 3/(3<sup>k</sup> ln(4/3)) ≈ 10<sup>-4</sup>.

claims.title: Does it halt?
claims.text: Not proved either way. By the kernel claims above, the question is exactly whether the orbit of (3, 1) under the hole map ever reaches p = 2 with r divisible by 3 (equivalently, a sample of length 3<sup>k</sup> + 1 with 3 | k followed by its division chain), a Collatz-like question with no visible invariant that rules it out.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now a clean number puzzle. Lean proves that this Turing machine halts exactly when a simple Collatz-like map, started from (3, 1), hits one particular case, and that it does not halt in its first 10<sup>3747</sup> steps. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and explains the map.

facts.text: No halt, proved in Lean by following the proved map.
The reduction, proved in Lean for all values.
Heuristic chance that it ever halts.

sections.heading: Ones with a single hole
html: Almost every cell this machine visits holds a 1. Each time the head is back at the left end (in state C, on a 1), the tape is N ones with exactly one 0, the hole, at position p. At step 800,549,613 for example:

Between two such moments the head bounces across the tape, moving the hole or extending the tape on the right by a cell per pair of sweeps: the square-root side. The left end grows by one cell per sample: since samples get rarer and rarer (N grows by a factor about 4/3 per sample, the time per sample like N2), the left side grows like a logarithm.

sections.eyebrow: The rule from one sample to the next
sections.heading: Divide by 3, or grow by a third
html:
• p ≡ 2 (mod 3), p ≥ 5: the hole jumps to (p − 2)/3 and N grows by 1;
  • p ≡ 0: the tape grows to N' = N + p/3 + 3 and the hole ends at N' − 2;
  • p ≡ 1: N' = N + (p − 1)/3 + 4, hole at N' − 2;
  • p = 2: if N is divisible by 3 the machine halts; otherwise the tape grows by 4 or 3.

Worked example from the run: (18,649, 18,647): 18,647 ≡ 2, so (18,650, 6,215); 6,215 ≡ 2, so (18,651, 2,071); 2,071 ≡ 1, so N' = 18,651 + 690 + 4 = 19,345 and the hole goes to 19,343, exactly what the machine does at step 1,071,541,900.

Proved for every N. Each case is a little machine of its own. For p = 3k+3, say, the head first builds a block 0 C> 1 (111)^k 0 next to the left end; one pass of 8k + 5 steps moves the whole block one cell to the right, past a 1; at the right end the block is eaten one 111 at a time, each bite leaving four 1s behind. For p ≡ 2 the head instead runs k division rounds, each turning a 111 into one 1 on the left of the hole and two 1s on its right, which is what divides the hole's position by 3. Each such pass is a rule found and proved automatically by bbtools.symtm; Lean then chains the passes by induction (the drift over all the ones, the k bites, the k rounds) and adds up the exact step counts (lean/Map.lean, theorem sample_step).

sections.heading: Only through 3<sup>k</sup> + 1
html: The halt is a real one: Lean proves that from C> 1 1 0 1^(3m+3) the machine halts after 5m + 22 steps, for every m. To get there the hole must reach position 2, and a division chain p → (p − 2)/3 → … ends at 2 only if it starts from 3k − 1. Chains start at N − 2 (or N − 3), so the run would have to land on a tape length of exactly 3k + 1 (and the length at the end of the chain must then be divisible by 3, which happens when 3 | k).

The lengths seen at the end-of-tape samples go 5, 9, 15, 23, 33, 47, …, 90,617 (step 1.9·1010), growing by about 4/3 each time; the map run 30,000 steps further (to numbers of 1,874 digits) never hits one. Treating the lengths as random at their scale, the chance of ever hitting one from here is about 10-4: probably it never halts, but this is a heuristic, not a proof.

What is proved. Lean proves that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the map, started from the first sample (p, r) = (3, 1) (the tape C> 1 1 1 0 1 at step 11), ever reaches p = 2 with r divisible by 3 (halts_iff). Following the proved map for 30,000 samples (the numbers then have 1,874 digits), Lean's kernel adds up the proved step counts: the machine does not halt in its first 103747 steps (no_halt_10_3747). The remaining question is about the numbers alone, and it looks as hard as the Collatz problem: nothing in the map rules out a lucky landing on 3k + 1.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.068). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.524).
After 109 steps the tape spans 18,652 cells (35 left of the start, 14,552 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.

summary: A tape of 1s with a single hole: a bouncer carries the hole to the right end, and each time it gets there the hole jumps to (p-2)/3 if its position p is 2 mod 3, else the tape grows by about a third; it halts exactly when a run of such divisions ends at position 2 with a length divisible by 3.
